vignette:
The client is a 58-year-old South Asian married male who presents for an initial diagnostic interview with symptoms consistent with posttraumatic stress disorder following his child’s life-threatening illness. He works as a bomb disposal technician, a profession that has required sustained exposure to high-risk situations and careful emotional control. He describes himself as “used to pressure,” though he appears noticeably tense throughout the interview and reports that his current symptoms feel different from the stress of his work. He is accompanied by a sense of burden and responsibility, and he states that his difficulties began after a prolonged medical crisis involving his child, during which he feared at multiple points that the child would not survive.

He reports intrusive memories of the illness and hospitalization, particularly moments when medical staff expressed concern that the condition could worsen suddenly. These recollections occur unexpectedly and are often triggered by sounds of medical equipment, hospital settings, or seeing his child fatigued or unwell. He describes vivid mental images of waiting for updates and feeling helpless while his child was “fighting to stay alive.” He denies full dissociative episodes but notes that when these memories arise, he experiences a surge of physiological distress including chest tightness, sweating, and a sense of impending doom. His PCL-5 score of 39 supports clinically significant posttraumatic symptoms.

The client endorses efforts to avoid reminders of the event. He says he limits conversations about the hospitalization and becomes uncomfortable when family members bring up details of the illness. He avoids visiting the hospital unless absolutely necessary and reports changing the subject when others ask how his child is doing. He recognizes that these patterns create distance within the family, though he frames the avoidance as a way of maintaining control and preventing himself from becoming overwhelmed. He also notes a reluctance to look through old photographs or medical documents related to the period of illness, stating that doing so “brings everything back.”

He describes persistent negative alterations in mood and cognition. Since the trauma, he has felt more guarded and emotionally restricted, with difficulty experiencing pleasure and a reduced sense of safety in daily life. He reports increased self-blame and recurrent thoughts that he should have done more to protect his child or recognized the severity of the illness earlier. Although he can acknowledge intellectually that the medical crisis was not his fault, he remains preoccupied with regret and with questions about whether his actions delayed treatment. He also expresses a sense of vulnerability that conflicts with his identity as a protective father and capable technician. He describes feeling “less steady” and worries that he is no longer fully reliable to his family.

The client endorses marked hyperarousal symptoms. He reports being more irritable than in the past, with a shorter fuse at home and increased sensitivity to minor frustrations. He notes sleep disruption, including difficulty falling asleep, frequent awakenings, and recurrent checking behaviors to ensure that family members are safe. He scans his surroundings more consistently and feels unable to fully relax, even in familiar environments. He also reports exaggerated startle responses to sudden sounds, which is particularly distressing given his occupation and his efforts to remain composed under pressure. He denies current substance misuse and denies suicidal ideation, intent, or plan. He does not report homicidal ideation.

Interpersonally, he appears deeply committed to his family but emotionally constricted. He and his spouse remain married and functionally stable, though he acknowledges increasing withdrawal and reduced communication during periods of stress. Cultural expectations around endurance, responsibility, and stoicism appear relevant to his presentation; he seems to view emotional disclosure as potentially burdensome to others and may have limited experience seeking support for psychological distress. He is able to engage respectfully in the interview and demonstrates intact insight, though he tends to minimize the extent of his suffering until prompted.

Overall, the client presents with a trauma-related syndrome characterized by intrusion, avoidance, negative mood and cognitions, and hyperarousal following his child’s life-threatening illness. His symptoms are causing clinically meaningful distress and are interfering with sleep, concentration, and family functioning. He appears motivated for treatment and may benefit from a trauma-focused approach that addresses guilt, hypervigilance, and the meaning he assigns to his role as a father and protector.
